content: The undergraduate and postgraduate programs aim to enhance the quantity, quality, and relevance of health professionals. 1. Database Searching: Pre-determined strategies were employed to search specific databases for relevant information. 2. Hand Searching: Relevant articles were manually searched in journals, websites, and resources, including the Journal of Nursing Administration, Journal of Continuing Education in Nursing, Journal for Nurses in Staff Development, Nursing Management, and the WHO Library Database (WHOLIS). 3. Expert Network Consultations: A network of experts in health professionals’ education was consulted via email to identify additional grey literature or research not captured through database or manual searches. 4. Reference Searches: Bibliographies of papers meeting eligibility criteria were manually reviewed to identify further relevant references. These references underwent the same screening and selection process. Eligibility Criteria: Types of Studies: All evaluative study designs, including grey literature, were eligible for inclusion. Methodological quality was not a criterion for selection. Types of Participants: Participants included those involved in health science educational programs for medical doctors (including public health doctors), nursing professionals (including public health nurses), midwifery professionals (including public health midwives), dentists, pharmacists, and health science students (e.g., medical, nursing, premedical, midwifery students, and residents). Practicing health professionals, including generalist and specialist medical doctors, nurses, midwives, dentists, pharmacists, and paramedical practitioners, were also included. Mid-level cadres such as assistant medical officers, clinical officers, health assistants, nurse clinicians, and physician assistants were considered. Types of Outcome Measures: Primary outcomes included the quantity, quality, and relevance of practicing health professionals, as defined by measurable outcomes in the Outcomes Framework document. Secondary outcomes included values, preferences, costs, benefits, harms, and unintended effects of interventions. Studies with other outcomes were not excluded at this stage. Exclusion Criteria: Editorials, newspaper articles, and other forms of popular media were excluded. Failure to meet any inclusion criteria resulted in exclusion. Discrepancies during the selection process were resolved by a third independent reviewer. Assessment of Risk of Bias and Data Extraction: After final selection, reviewers extracted data using pre-defined evidence summary templates. Data included reasons for exclusion, characteristics of included studies, participants, interventions (including comparators), and outcomes. Final inclusion or exclusion decisions were made by a team comprising the WHO Secretariat, methodologists, and researchers. Disagreements were recorded and resolved through further discussion. Risk of bias across studies was assessed using the GRADE approach. Data Synthesis: The feasibility of conducting a meta-analysis was considered based on the availability of appropriate data and resources. Dissemination: A final set of tables, including GRADE evidence and descriptive evidence, was submitted to the WHO Secretariat. A manuscript will also be submitted to peer-reviewed journals for publication. Resource Implications: The project lead collaborated with the WHO Secretariat to define the scope and methods of the review, facilitate access to unpublished literature, and support the translation of foreign-language literature when necessary. References: The references cited include a wide range of studies and reports on clinical ladder programs, career advancement initiatives, and health manpower development strategies. These references provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding the effectiveness and implementation of such programs in various healthcare settings.
